Field notes · Letter

A nurse, a surgeon and a wooden doll

Three stories that turn out to be one, and what they say about the top of a nest of boards.

DJ, founderNovember 9, 20263 min read

Brooklyn, 11:02 p.m.

Somewhere in Brooklyn right now, a triage nurse is working the front desk of an emergency room. She gets a minute or two with each person. A man with a dish towel wrapped around his hand. A teenager who can’t stop coughing. A woman who says she’s fine and isn’t.

She won’t fix any of them. Her job is to decide what happens next.

A field hospital, the 1790s

Two hundred years earlier, a surgeon in Napoleon’s army did something his officers found outrageous. When the wounded came in, he sorted them by how badly they were hurt, not by rank. A general with a scratch waited behind a private who was bleeding out. The French verb for sorting is trier, and the word stuck.

A workshop outside Moscow, the 1890s

A carver turns a block of wood into a round little woman, and a painter gives her a face. She splits at the waist. Inside is a smaller woman, and inside her a smaller one, down to a doll the size of a bean.

The outer doll is the only one most people ever see. She shows one calm face and keeps everything else a layer down.

Brooklyn, 11:05 p.m.

The man with the towel waits. The woman who says she’s fine goes straight back. Nobody in the waiting room likes the order, and the order is right.

My desk, 11:06 p.m.

A link lands on my home board. That’s where everything new goes: loose, outside the three regions that are the only things on the board. Now holds the two or three boards I’m actually in the middle of. Soon holds what’s waiting its turn. Resting holds what’s done but not put away.

I don’t open the link yet. First, where does it go?

All of it, at once

Where does this go next? It’s the nurse’s question at 11:02, and the surgeon’s two hundred years ago. The doll answers the other half: show one calm face, and keep the rest a layer down.

Whatever sits on top of a lot of things, an emergency room or a set of dolls or a nest of boards, has one job. It shows one calm face, and it decides what goes next. Every board under my home board is about something: a move, a trip, a book. The home board is about attention.

This letter started as one of those loose cards, a note I typed one night: “ER triage = home board?” I sorted it into Soon. This is what it turned into.

Yours doesn’t have to be a triage desk. It might be a shelf, or a wall for the week. Whatever sits at the top sets how everything under it feels.

So, what’s on your home board?
